description: Width tiers for Foundation Mathematics — ACARA v9. One entry per descriptor code.
subject: Mathematics

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest context or phenomenon that honestly meets the Foundation descriptor's command term. Set by the verb — recognise, name, sort, sequence, describe. Minimum is singular in focus.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended, grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects what a well-taught Foundation class would have engaged with.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts or cultural connections — not harder versions of the same activity. Includes First Nations contexts where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are examples, not a syllabus. Used to ground typical_width and identify First Nations directions. Wider may infer beyond elaborations where clearly within the descriptor's territory.

AC9MFA01.minimum_width: Recognise and copy a repeating pattern using one type of material (e.g. coloured beads or shapes), identifying what element is being repeated.
AC9MFA01.typical_width: Recognise, copy and continue repeating patterns across a range of materials, shapes, sounds and movements; describe what is being repeated using everyday language; connect patterns to familiar routines and activities.
wider: Recognise and describe repeating patterns generated by dynamic geometric software or a generative AI tool, identifying what has been repeated in the pattern
Create original repeating patterns using combinations of two or more attributes (colour and shape, sound and movement)

Recognise and describe repeating patterns observed on Country/Place and in First Nations Australians' artwork, cultural performances and material cultures (e.g. shell and seed necklaces, dances, songs)
elaborations: recognising, copying and describing different repeating patterns using materials, shapes, sounds and movements during activities and play; for example, making a bead necklace and describing the pattern they have created, such as, red, blue, green, red, blue, green, red, blue, green; copying repeating patterns of drumbeats or dance moves during music activities
recognising repeating patterns used at home and in daily activities to help make tasks easier or to solve problems; for example, setting the table to eat
recognising and discussing repeating patterns in images created using dynamic geometric software or a generative artificial intelligence tool, describing what has been repeated in the pattern

recognising and describing repeating patterns that can be observed on Country/Place and in First Nation Australians artwork, cultural performances and material cultures; for example, shell and seed necklaces, dances and songs

AC9MFM01.minimum_width: Directly compare two objects on a single measurement attribute (length or mass or capacity) and use appropriate language to describe the comparison (e.g. longer/shorter, heavier/lighter, holds more/less).
AC9MFM01.typical_width: Identify and compare objects and events across all four measurement attributes (length, mass, capacity, duration) using direct comparison; use appropriate measurement language for each attribute; communicate reasoning about comparisons using familiar terms.
wider: Compare the same pair of objects across two different attributes (e.g. which is longer AND which is heavier), discussing how different attributes give different information
Explore how measurement language connects to familiar contexts and actions at home and in the community, including comparing objects found on Country/Place
Investigate how objects that look similar can differ on a measurement attribute (e.g. two similar-looking containers that hold different amounts), prompting reasoning about why
elaborations: using language to describe the measurement attributes of length, mass, capacity and duration, and connecting the words with the appropriate attribute; for example, using words like 'tall', 'short', 'wide', 'long', 'high' to describe the attribute of length

directly comparing pairs of objects to say which is longer/shorter, and explaining or demonstrating how they know; for example, standing back-to-back to determine who is taller; choosing to line up the bases of a spoon and fork to decide which is longer and explaining why
starting 2 events at the same time to decide which takes longer; for example, putting on a pair of sandals with buckles or Velcro, describing the duration using familiar terms and reasoning

directly comparing pairs of everyday objects from the kitchen pantry to say which is heavier/lighter; for example, hefting a tin of baked beans and a packet of marshmallows; comparing the same pair of objects to say which is longer/shorter and discussing comparisons

AC9MFM02.minimum_width: Sequence the days of the week in order and connect at least one familiar event to a specific time of day (morning, lunchtime, afternoon or night).
AC9MFM02.typical_width: Sequence days of the week and times of day; connect familiar school and home events to the correct day and time; use positional language (before, after, next, yesterday, today, tomorrow) to describe event sequences; recognise that the days of the week repeat.
wider: Create and interpret classroom rosters or pictorial diaries connecting events to specific days, reasoning about who did what and when
Sequence events from a story in the order they occurred, using temporal language to justify the placement
Explore how different families or communities organise their week (including school days vs weekends, cultural or community events on specific days) and discuss similarities and differences
elaborations: ordering images of daily events on a string line across the room, and justifying the placement by referring to morning, lunchtime, afternoon, and night time
distinguishing between the days of the school week and weekends, and recognising that the days of the week form a sequence that repeats, with Monday always following on from Sunday
sequencing the events from a story in the order in which they occurred using language like, 'This happened first' then 'This happened next'
creating, interpreting and discussing classroom rosters; for example, a roster for watering the classroom garden
creating a pictorial diary to show the important events that happen on the various days of the week

AC9MFN01.minimum_width: Name and represent numbers to at least 10 using physical materials or numerals; identify a given quantity by selecting the matching numeral or collection.
AC9MFN01.typical_width: Name, represent and order numbers including zero to at least 20 using physical and virtual materials and numerals; identify one more and one less; use ordinal language (first, second, third) to describe positions; recognise and write numerals in familiar contexts.
wider: Explore numbers to 20 on different representations (number tracks, number lines, ten-frames, fingers) and connect between representations
Connect quantities to number names and numerals through First Nations Australians' counting contexts — e.g. Segur etug from Mer Island in the Torres Strait region
Use instructive card games (e.g. ordering number cards, reading and placing numerals) that involve reading, ordering and connecting numerals to quantities beyond 20
elaborations: responding to a request to collect a quantity of objects or reading a numeral and selecting the associated quantity of items from a collection

recognising the order in the sequence of numbers to 20 and identifying the number that is 'one less' than a given number and the number that is 'one more'; playing instructive card games; using counting songs, story books and rhymes
understanding and using terms such as 'first', 'second', 'third', to indicate ordinal position in a sequence
recognising, writing and reading numerals written on familiar objects
connecting quantities to number names and numerals when reading and reciting stories and playing counting games; Segur etug from Mer Island in the Torres Strait region

AC9MFN02.minimum_width: Recognise the number of objects in a collection up to 5 with a quick look, without counting, and name the number.
AC9MFN02.typical_width: Recognise and name the number of objects in collections up to 5 using subitising in a range of arrangements; use subitising to compare and order small collections; recognise numbers represented in different ways (dot cards, dice patterns, dominoes).
wider: Use subitising to play instructive card games that rely on matching quantities in different arrangements (e.g. memory games with dot cards where arrangements differ)
Investigate structured subitising of numbers up to 5 represented in part-part combinations (e.g. 4 as 3+1 or 2+2) to connect subitising to early part-part-whole thinking
Explore how subitising is used in everyday life contexts — e.g. dice games, dominoes, tally marks — and describe the strategy
AC9MFN02.width_notes: Thin width — subitising to 5 does not vary greatly across contexts. Wider items add representational variety and connections rather than new phenomena.
elaborations: recognising how many objects are in a collection or in images on a card with a quick look and saying the associated number without counting

playing instructive card games that rely on the recognition of numbers represented in different ways; for example, playing memory games, matching pairs of quantities on dot cards or similar where the arrangement on each is different; using subitising to compare and order collections

AC9MFN03.minimum_width: Count a collection of up to 10 objects accurately using one-to-one correspondence, demonstrating that the last number counted tells how many.
AC9MFN03.typical_width: Quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting; apply one-to-one correspondence and demonstrate that arrangement does not affect quantity; use counting to compare collections and justify which has more or less; use counting for practical purposes (e.g. collecting the right number of items for a group).
wider: Explore body-tallying counting systems from First Nations Peoples of Australia that use body parts and one-to-one correspondence to count to 20
Investigate how different cultures represent counts — e.g. an abacus or Chinese hand gestures — and connect these to the counting sequence
Extend counting beyond 20 to explore what happens to the sequence, making predictions and testing them with collections or counting materials
elaborations: establishing the language and process of counting, understanding that each object must be counted only once, that the arrangement of objects does not affect how many there are, and that the last number counted answers the question of 'How many?'
using counting to compare the size of two or more collections of like items to justify which collection contains more or less items
using counting and one-to-one correspondence to quantify the number of items required for a purpose
discussing how different cultures may have alternative ways of representing the count; for example, discussing how people of the Asia region use an abacus or Chinese hand gestures
using body-tallying that involves body parts and one-to-one correspondence from counting systems of First Nations Peoples of Australia, to count to 20

AC9MFN04.minimum_width: Partition a collection of up to 10 objects into two parts and name both parts and the whole (e.g. '6 is 4 and 2').
AC9MFN04.typical_width: Partition and combine collections up to 10 in multiple ways using physical or virtual materials; use subitising to recognise parts within a whole (ten-frames, dominoes, dice); name part-part-whole relationships; explore different partitions of the same number.
wider: Explore First Nations Australians' counting systems and the different ways of representing groupings to form and partition numbers — applying this to quantify collections of objects in the environment on Country/Place up to 10
Use a range of structured representations (ten-frames, rekenreks, dot cards) to partition numbers and compare which representations make particular partitions easier to see
Investigate all the ways to partition numbers to 10 systematically, connecting to later addition and subtraction thinking
elaborations: recognising numbers represented in physical or virtual ten-frames, and describing their reasoning
partitioning collections of up to 10 objects in different ways and saying the part-part-whole relationship
representing part-part-whole relationships in numbers up to 10 using physical or virtual materials; identifying numbers represented by dots in standard number configurations such as dominos and dice

exploring number groupings in First Nations Australians' counting systems and the different ways of representing these groupings to form and partition numbers, applying this to quantify collections up to 10

AC9MFN05.minimum_width: Represent one practical addition or subtraction situation using materials or a drawing, and use counting to find the result.
AC9MFN05.typical_width: Represent a range of practical situations involving addition and subtraction using physical or virtual materials; use counting or subitising strategies to quantify results; connect representations to everyday contexts including simple quantity comparisons and money situations.
wider: Represent addition and subtraction situations from First Nations Australians' stories (e.g. 'Tiddalick the Greedy Frog') and leaf games from the Warlpiri Peoples of Yuendumu — describing the additive situation and its connection to Country/Place
Role-play simple money transactions using $1 coins, representing the situation with materials and finding the result through counting
Explore story-based additive situations across different familiar contexts (animals, classroom objects, food) and compare how the same mathematical relationship appears in different stories
elaborations: using role-play and materials to represent mathematical relationships in stories; drawing a picture and using materials to represent the situation
role playing or actively engaging in situations that involve quantifying or comparing collections of items or simple money transactions
representing situations expressed in First Nations Australians' stories, such as 'Tiddalick, the greedy frog', that describe additive situations and their connections to Country/Place
representing addition and subtraction situations found in leaf games involving sets of objects used to tell stories, such as games from the Warlpiri Peoples of Yuendumu in the Northern Territory

AC9MFN06.minimum_width: Represent one equal-sharing situation using materials, share a collection into equal groups, and use counting to check each group has the same amount.
AC9MFN06.typical_width: Represent practical situations involving equal sharing and grouping using physical or virtual materials across a range of everyday contexts; use counting or subitising to determine the size of each equal group; justify equal distribution.
wider: Explore instructive games of First Nations Australians involving equal sharing — e.g. Yangamini of the Tiwi Peoples of Bathurst Island — investigating and discussing what makes sharing equal
Compare sharing scenarios where quantities do not share equally (remainders at Foundation level) and discuss what happens to the leftovers
Investigate grouping contexts (putting items in groups of the same size) alongside sharing contexts, connecting both to the idea of equal groups
elaborations: using materials to role-play equal sharing; for example, sharing pieces of fruit or a bunch of grapes between 4 people
representing situations that involve counting several items and sharing them equally between 3 people by subitising or counting each group by ones
exploring instructive games of First Nations Australians that involve sharing; for example, playing Yangamini of the Tiwi Peoples of Bathurst Island

AC9MFSP01.minimum_width: Name at least three familiar shapes (e.g. circle, triangle, rectangle/square) and sort a collection of shapes by one attribute (e.g. number of sides or shape name).
AC9MFSP01.typical_width: Sort, name and create familiar shapes using a range of materials; recognise and describe familiar shapes within objects in the environment; sort shapes by different features (number of sides, colour, size); give reasons for sorting decisions.
wider: Describe and name shapes observed on Country/Place, recreate them and sort into groups based on their shape — connecting mathematics to the environment and First Nations contexts
Create pictures or patterns using combinations of shapes, describing each shape chosen and explaining why it was selected
Investigate three-dimensional objects and identify the two-dimensional faces that make them up, connecting 2D shape knowledge to 3D objects in the environment
elaborations: sorting a collection of shapes into groups based on different features such as the number of sides, colour or size, and describing how they have been sorted
creating a picture using a variety of shapes and a range of materials, including objects to trace around, describing the shapes they have created or used
creating familiar shapes using groups of people; for example, holding hands and creating a circle
recognising and naming shapes that are (close to) rectangles, squares, triangles and circles in component parts of everyday items
describing and naming shapes within objects that can be observed on Country/Place, recreating and sorting into groups based on their shape

AC9MFSP02.minimum_width: Describe the position of one object in relation to another using at least one positional word (e.g. 'in', 'on', 'under', 'next to', 'behind').
AC9MFSP02.typical_width: Describe the position and location of themselves and objects in relation to other people and objects using a range of positional language (inside, underneath, on top of, behind, next to, near, far); describe movement of themselves and objects within a familiar space.
wider: Explore First Nations Australians' instructive games — e.g. Thapumpan from the Wik-Mungkan Peoples of Cape Bedford in north Queensland — describing position and movement of self in relation to other participants, objects or locations
Use positional language to describe the movement of a robotic toy as it moves around a space, connecting spatial language to technology contexts
Create simple location descriptions for familiar spaces (the classroom, the playground) and test whether others can follow them to find a hidden object
elaborations: describing the position of an item in relation to other items in the space using language like 'inside', 'underneath' and 'on top of'
describing where they have moved themselves and items in relation to other items within a space, using familiar terms
describing the position of a robotic toy in relation to other objects as it moves around a familiar space

exploring First Nations Australians' instructive games; for example, Thapumpan from the Wik-Mungkan Peoples of Cape Bedford in north Queensland, describing position and movement of self in relation to other participants

AC9MFST01.minimum_width: Collect objects or images in response to one given investigative question and sort them into two groups; compare the groups to answer the question.
AC9MFST01.typical_width: Collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images in response to given investigative questions; organise data to answer yes/no and comparison questions; create simple classroom charts using objects or stickers; interpret and compare representations.
wider: Explore what and how information from the environment is collected and used by First Nations Australians to predict weather events — connecting data collection to Country/Place knowledge
Role-play training an AI system to recognise objects by asking yes/no questions to gather data — connecting data collection to digital and AI contexts
Investigate statistical contexts from picture books (e.g. 'The Waterhole' by Graeme Base) — generating investigative questions, collecting data from the book, and comparing results
elaborations: collecting, and sorting data collected through everyday activities or events; for example, sorting toys into categories
collecting and deciding how to organise data to answer 'Yes/No' questions
creating classroom charts and rosters using stickers to represent data; comparing and interpreting representations
role-playing being a robot that sorts objects into groups based on a set of instructions
role-playing, as a class, at training an artificial intelligence system to recognise objects
investigating statistical contexts after reading a story, such as 'The Waterhole' by Graeme Base
exploring what and how information from the environment is collected and used by First Nations Australians to predict weather events
